The estimated annual effective inhalation doses for workers near or even above locally recommended occupational safety levels may be pointed to an increased risk of cancer over a worker's lifetime. These results highlight the urgent need for effective dust management, better ventilation, proper use of personal protective equipment, and regular radiation monitoring that specifically addresses inhalation exposure. Overall, this research sheds light on the occupational and environmental exposure risks linked to natural radioactive phosphate mining and will help develop strategies for better environmental and occupational radiation protection.

title: A predictive model for acid generation critical time in filtered tailings using acidification and neutralization potential
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry, Volume 208 Author(s): Corentin Chevalier, Thomas Pabst, Isabelle Demers
abstract: Tailings filtration enhances the geotechnical stability of tailings storage facilities and contributes to reducing their overall footprint. However, despite these operational advantages, the low degree of saturation associated with filtered tailings may also increase the risk for acid mine drainage (AMD) generation. In this research, laboratory kinetic tests were coupled with multicomponent reactive transport simulations to assess the time tailings can remain exposed before AMD generation starts, identified as critical time. Laboratory kinetics tests were performed on reactive mine tailings at various degrees of saturation, and the evolution of pore-water geochemistry was monitored over time. Numerical simulations were then calibrated on the laboratory tests and extrapolated to other mineral contents. Experimental and numerical results showed that critical time was significantly delayed when the degree of saturation exceeded 90%. The critical time was primarily governed by the neutralization potential associated with carbonate content, and was also influenced by the net neutralization potential, especially when neutralization to acidification potential ratio was greater than 0.5. Finally, a predictive equation was proposed to estimate critical time. Predicting critical time can be useful to optimize filtered tailings management and reclamation and improve the geochemical stability of filtered tailings storage facilities.

title: Soil aggregate fractionation modulates Mollisol organic carbon biomineralization and CO 2 emission during freeze-thaw cycles
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry, Volume 208 Author(s): Wenjuan Zou, Kunfu Pi, Hongyan Li, Qianyong Liang, Lifen Liu, Fereidoun Rezanezhad
abstract: Freeze-thaw cycles (FTCs) strongly regulate soil carbon dynamics in cold regions. Soil aggregates are core structural units that protect soil organic carbon (SOC) and regulate its biomineralization. While previous studies provide a good understanding of bulk soil properties, it remains elusive how aggregate size distribution modulates SOC biomineralization under repeated freeze-thaw cycles (FTCs). Cold-region Mollisols, which are characterized by high SOC concentration and strong aggregation, provide an ideal system to address this gap. Destructuring Mollisol aggregates enables disentangling size-dependent carbon protection mechanisms for preventing SOC from biodegradation. Here, joint field investigations and controlled FTCs incubation experiments were conducted using physically separated Mollisol aggregates to disentangle size-dependent carbon protection mechanisms. The results present new evidence that aggregate-mediated SOC biomineralization under FTCs exhibits a pronounced size-dependent pattern. Large macroaggregates (LMA) experienced severe physical disintegration during FTCs, exposing protected SOC and releasing 40% - 60% more cumulative CO2 than microaggregates (MIA). Small macroaggregates (SMA) showed moderate structural breakdown but comparatively low SOC biomineralization due to biochemical constraints. MIA remained structurally stable, accumulated microbially-derived dissolved organic matter, and acted as a stable carbon sink through organo-mineral associations and microbial adaptation. A modified dual-pool kinetic model further reveals that SOC loss from LMA was primarily driven by physical fragmentation, while SOC retention in MIA was governed by chemical stabilization and microbial resilience. Overall, our results highlight that aggregate hierarchical structure exerts critical control on SOC turnover and CO2 emission in cold-region Mollisols. Carbon biogeochemical models should integrate aggregate-level processes to accurately predict soil carbon dynamics in cold-region terrestrial ecosystems.

title: Iron precipitation for permeability reduction of sands
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry, Volume 208 Author(s): Zachary Hubbard, Sahil Kanawade, Leon van Paassen, Cesar I. Torres
abstract: We present in this paper an approach to reduce sand permeability through the aerobic precipitation of ferric iron. First, a passive, counterdiffusion approach in which de-oxygenated water with Fe(II) chloride and an organic buffer (either sodium acetate or sodium propionate) is employed to saturate the sand. As oxidation proceeds, aqueous iron is consumed and a band of precipitate forms below the sand-air interface. This establishes a gradient in which iron diffuses upwards toward the source of oxygen to fuel further oxidation. Secondly, an active, flush-based approach involving the periodic introduction/draining of treatment solution was employed in attempt to overcome caveats of counterdiffusion. In these tests, water is periodically cycled every 30 min. This allows air to fully permeate the columns, provides enhanced control over the reaction environment, and enables oxidation and precipitation over a greater depth. Various initial concentrations of iron ranging from 0.1 M to 1 M in concentration were assessed. Using these approaches, the hydraulic conductivity of Ottawa 20-30 sand has been reduced by 22% to 98%, with the extent of reduction correlating positively with the concentration of iron. The use of propionate as a buffer generally led to higher reductions in permeability—a result attributed to decreased complexation with iron relative to acetate. Counterdiffusion experiments, while offering a simple and passive approach and successfully reducing permeability in some cases by up to 98% while requiring fewer reagents, often resulted in a thin and easily fractured layer at lower concentrations. The flush approach, while enhancing oxygenation and allocating precipitates over an extended region, inspired a rapid reaction and precipitates which more-readily detached from sand prior to elution during hydraulic conductivity tests.

title: Enhanced mineral carbonation of CO 2 in basalt using circulating fluidized bed combustion fly ash
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry, Volume 208 Author(s): Junbeum Lee, Sangyong Bae, Kyeongmin Kim, Geonhee Jang, Sangkeon Park, Hanna Ryu, Hoonyoung Jeong, Eunhyea Chung
abstract: Of the various CO2 trapping mechanisms, mineral carbonation is considered one of the most secure approaches for long-term geological carbon storage. Basaltic formations are attractive due to their abundance of Ca- and Mg-bearing minerals; however, mineral carbonation is often limited by insufficient release of reactive Ca ions. Here, circulating fluidized bed combustion (CFBC) fly ash was evaluated as an additional Ca source to enhance mineral carbonation in basaltic systems. Batch experiments using 0.64 M Na2CO3 showed no detectable carbonate formation in the basalt system consistent with XRD results and a low total carbon content of 0.18 %. In contrast, the addition of CFBC fly ash resulted in calcite formation and increased total carbon content up to 11.22 %. A reference system composed of CaCl2·2H2O and Na2CO3 showed a higher carbon content of 15.56 %, thus confirming the formation of carbonate precipitates under Ca-rich conditions. Geochemical modeling based on batch conditions showed that the calcite saturation index (SI) increased from 0.53 to 3.41 with CFBC fly ash addition under alkaline conditions. Under CO2-rich conditions, increasing CO2 pressure (up to 5 MPa) decreased pH from 9.84 to 5.46 and reduced calcite SI from 3.46 to 0.67 due to carbonate speciation shifts. These results demonstrate that mineral carbonation in basaltic systems is primarily controlled by Ca availability in Na2CO3-based alkaline systems, whereas under CO2 (g)-rich conditions, pH and carbonate speciation govern mineral stability and precipitation behavior.

title: Unravelling the functioning of andesitic volcanic aquifers in the equatorial zone using isotopic, age-dating and geochemical tracers
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry, Volume 208 Author(s): Antoine Picard, Florent Barbecot, Lucas Jurain, Patrick Lachassagne, Nicolas Patris, Jürgen Sültenfuß, Arif Fadillah, Azwar Satrya Muhammad, Nathalie Dörfliger, Heru Hendrayana
abstract: The hydrogeological structure of volcanic aquifers is now rather well known, including for andesitic systems. However, despite the existence of well-established Hydrogeological Conceptual Models (HCM), the functioning of andesitic aquifers remains insufficiently understood. Environmental tracers provide valuable tools to address this issue. In this study, we applied a multi-tracer approach combining hydrochemistry, water stable isotopes (δ 2H – δ 18O) and tritium (3H) in the Kedunglarangan watershed (Pandaan, Indonesia). This combination of tracers enabled a refined delineation of groundwater recharge areas by introducing a bilinear model accounting for secondary evaporation effects. We also propose a continuous (from 1900 to present) 3H input function for the equatorial Asian region. The generic HCM of andesitic volcanic aquifers and their hydrogeological functioning were significantly improved through the identification of seven groundwater groups based on tracer signatures and groundwater age modelling. At high elevations, volcanic edifices host unconfined aquifers recharged locally through permeable lava flows and characterized by short residence times ( 25 years), although few systems show evidence of substantial local recharge from lower elevations. Further downstream, within the volcano-sedimentary plain, confined aquifers overlain by lahars naturally discharge through large springs fed predominantly by high-elevation recharge, with variable but higher mean residence times (>50 years). In addition, several shallow locally recharged aquifers display low recharge rates and relatively long residence times (>100 years), discharging through small springs. This zone is also characterized by the occurrence of very old hydrothermal waters outflowing near outcropping deep geological structures. These results demonstrate a clear hydrogeological continuity from the top of the volcanoes to their feet that could not be demonstrated based only on structural (geology) and hydrodynamic information. This research greatly improves the understanding of recharge dynamics and groundwater flow circulation in recent andesitic volcanic systems. Beyond the local case, the methodology provides tools that can be used for groundwater budget assessment and groundwater quality protection in similar volcanic contexts worldwide (e.g. Pacific Ring of Fire, Caribbean, Mediterranean volcanoes etc.).

title: Phosphate and nitrate isotope responses to lateral plume mixing and nutrient turnover downstream of a wastewater discharge
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry, Volume 208 Author(s): Daren C. Gooddy, Michael J. Bowes, Alexandra V.E. O'Brien, David J.E. Nicholls, Andi C. Smith, James P.R. Sorensen, Patrick Harrison, Stefan Krause
abstract: Wastewater treatment works (WwTW) are major point sources of nutrients to rivers, but interpretation of downstream isotope signals is complicated where hydrodynamic mixing and in-stream biogeochemical processing occur over similar spatial scales. Here, we combine phosphate oxygen isotopes (δ18O-PO4), nitrate nitrogen and oxygen isotopes (δ15N–NO3 and δ18O–NO3), and nutrient concentrations to investigate nutrient behaviour over a short River Thames, UK reach downstream of a WwTW discharge. The study resolves a high-resolution spatial pattern from a single sampling survey and is framed within a two-dimensional mixing context, in which effluent-influenced water and background river water are transported downstream in parallel rather than as a laterally well-mixed one-dimensional system. Phosphate concentrations and δ18O-PO4 values showed a strong response to the effluent input. Near the outfall, isotope compositions were broadly consistent with conservative mixing between effluent and river phosphate, with first-order estimates suggesting that effluent-derived phosphate contributed approximately 20–55% of the local dissolved inorganic phosphate pool at plume-influenced sampling points. Further downstream, several δ18O-PO4 values were close to the independently calculated temperature-dependent equilibrium composition of approximately 17.2‰, consistent with possible biological isotope resetting of phosphate within the reach. However, because travel times and turnover rates were not directly measured, this convergence is interpreted as evidence for short-reach isotope resetting rather than as a quantified rate of biological turnover. A pronounced low δ18O-PO4 value at approximately 220 m downstream fell outside the range predicted using the measured effluent end member, indicating end-member uncertainty or plume heterogeneity within the wastewater-influenced water mass. In contrast, nitrate concentrations and isotope compositions showed little spatial variation downstream of the discharge. δ15N–NO3 and δ18O–NO3 displayed no coupled downstream enrichment, indicating no detectable isotopic evidence for substantial denitrification over the sampled reach and hydrological conditions. However, the large background nitrate pool means that local nitrogen transformations, including nitrification, assimilation or localised denitrification, may have been difficult to resolve. These contrasting isotope responses show that phosphate was sensitive to both local plume structure and possible biological isotope resetting, whereas nitrate primarily reflected buffering by a large background nitrate pool. More broadly, the results demonstrate that interpretation of river nutrient isotope signals below point-source inputs requires explicit consideration of lateral hydrodynamic structure, end-member uncertainty and nutrient-specific reactivity.

title: Inter-basin groundwater flow pathways and hydrogeochemical evolution regulated by deep fault systems
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry, Volume 208 Author(s): Xiaoyan Shi, Xingxing Kuang, Meizhuang Zhu, Linfeng Fan, Gexi Zheng, Xinkang Wang, Jianxin Chen, Yinlei Hao, Xiaolang Zhang, Chunmiao Zheng
abstract: Inter-basin groundwater flow (IGF) is defined as groundwater flow across topographic or hydrologic basin boundaries, which plays a critical role in regional water budgets and the global water cycle. On the Tibetan Plateau (TP), IGF has been acknowledged as the primary process responsible for water deficits of drainage basins, with deep fault systems serving as the principal conduits facilitating such flow. This study presents comprehensive hydrogeochemical and multi-isotopic evidence (δ18O, δ2H, 3H, 87Sr/86Sr, and trace elements) to delineate fault-controlled IGF in the southern TP. The results demonstrate that a portion of the leakage water from Nam Co Lake migrates southward as IGF into adjacent river basins along deep, middle, and shallow pathways constrained by the underlying deep fault system. The hydrogeochemical evolution of deep IGF is characterized by inputs from magmatic fluids and extensive interactions with carbonate and silicate minerals, while shallower pathways are primarily controlled by carbonate dissolution and freshwater mixing. These findings underscore the significance of deep faults in regulating IGF transport and evolution. A ternary mixing model of 87Sr/86Sr and δ18O indicates that IGF mixing ratios in local groundwater range from 1.0% to 26.5%, generally decreasing with flow distance. The contribution of IGF to river runoff is estimated to be <6.0% compared with the dominant sources of meteoric water and local groundwater. This study presents a hydrogeochemical framework for identifying IGF patterns beyond water-balance approaches, providing valuable insights into regional water resource assessment and sustainable management on the TP and in other fault-controlled areas.

title: Dissolved oxygen control on manganese release and component-selective DOM transport at the sediment–water interface: A mechanistic geochemical study of lake biwa sediments
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry, Volume 208 Author(s): Yasuro Fuse, Hitomi Tsuda, Hiroko Okuda, Xue Chu, Yasuhiko T. Yamaguchi, Kazuhide Hayakawa
abstract: Bottom-water deoxygenation is intensifying in many stratified lakes, yet quantitative links between dissolved oxygen (DO) and sediment redox fluxes and dissolved organic matter (DOM) exchange remain uncertain. Here we used long-duration intact-core incubations from Lake Biwa (Japan) under three controlled DO regimes (0, 2.6, and 10 mg L−1 at 7°C) to evaluate how DO modulates Mn/Fe/P mobility and the relative transport/retention of humic-like vs protein-like fluorescent DOM components. Anoxia triggered large Mn release (to ∼40 mg L−1 by day 120), whereas 2.6 and 10 mg L−1 suppressed Mn to ≤0.5 mg L−1 (∼130× lower). In contrast, dissolved Fe and P remained low across treatments (<0.5 and < 0.3 mg L−1). Fluorescence excitation–emission matrices (EEMs) showed preferential accumulation of protein-like signals in pore waters, while fulvic acid–like (FA-like) signals were more evident in overlying waters. Nernst/Gibbs calculations yield a thermodynamic ordering consistent with preferential Mn reduction before Fe under our experimental conditions, though this interpretation remains a working hypothesis pending direct verification. We emphasize that our incubations represent a gas-controlled, closed-water design that excludes bioturbation and advective transport, and that fluorescence classes are operational proxies rather than direct molecular-size measurements. Together, these results provide testable, physicochemically grounded hypotheses for DO-sensitive Mn cycling and DOM partitioning at sediment–water interfaces in stratified lakes.

title: A mineral-centric framework for predicting arsenic behaviour in lithium mine wastes
description: Publication date: Available online 3 September 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry Author(s): Quentin Bollaert, Quentin Dehaine, Fernando Prado Araujo, Sonja Lavikko, Hugh O’Brien, Olivier Mathon, Valérie Cappuyns
abstract: The expansion of lithium mining in Europe is essential for securing strategic raw materials, but it raises increasing challenges for long-term tailings management. Arsenic (As), present at trace levels in lithium ores, can partition into mine wastes during beneficiation, yet its mineral hosts and solid-phase speciation remain poorly constrained due to low concentrations and diffuse distribution. This limits predictions of arsenic behaviour during processing, leaching, and storage, while current assessments often rely on bulk data that overlook key mineralogical controls. Here, we combine quantitative mineral deportment with As K-edge XANES to characterise arsenic distribution and speciation in ores and residues from three major European lithium projects. Arsenic occurs across sulfide, sulfarsenide, silicate, oxide, and phosphate phases, typically at trace levels but within abundant minerals. Sulfarsenides are dominated by As(–I), whereas other phases show mixed speciation (As(–I), As(III), As(V)). Linear combination fitting indicates overall dominance of As(–I) and As(V), with As(III) minor and sample-specific. XANES of leaching residues reveal the oxidation of arsenic released during arsenopyrite dissolution to As(V), followed by its immobilisation under specific pH conditions, demonstrating that arsenic leaching behaviour at disposal sites is strongly controlled by weathering conditions. Coupled with traditional leaching approaches, this mineral-centric framework quantifies the contribution of As-bearing phases and their control on release across environments, supporting more targeted tailings management and improved environmental strategies for lithium production.

title: Enhanced stacking ensemble learning for predicting fluoride and iodine contamination in groundwater of the lower Yellow River floodplain, Northern China
description: Publication date: Available online 3 September 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry Author(s): Shishan Xing, Chuanshun Zhi, Xiaonong Hu, Wenbo Chang, Ruchun Wei, Yuxi Li, Hongnian Chen, Hongliang Li, Yulong Dong, Guangwei Wu, Wenwen Bi
abstract: Geogenic fluoride (F–) and iodine (I–) contamination in groundwater poses a persistent threat to public health and the sustainability of drinking-water supply systems, particularly in data-scarce regions where preventive management remains challenging. However, effective groundwater management is often constrained by fragmented monitoring networks and limited decision-support tools capable of translating complex environmental information into actionable risk guidance. In this study, we develop an explainable decision-support framework to support sustainable groundwater management by integrating enhanced stacking ensemble learning, SHAP-based interpretation, and self-organizing maps (SOM). Using 292 groundwater samples and 40 environmental predictors, exceedance probabilities of F– (≥1.0 mg/L) and I– (≥0.08 mg/L) were mapped across the lower Yellow River floodplain, Northern China. The optimized stacking models achieved high predictive performance, with AUC values of 0.94 for F– and 0.92 for I–. Spatial predictions reveal distinct yet overlapping high-risk belts, with 43% of the region exposed to elevated fluoride risk and 57% to iodine risk, indicating that nearly half of the floodplain faces long-term groundwater quality constraints. Feature attribution analysis demonstrates that hydrochemical conditions dominate contamination risk, while hydrogeology, sedimentary environment, climate, human activities and soil physicochemical properties further regulate spatial heterogeneity. SOM clustering further clarified the coupled effects of hydrogeological settings and geochemical processes on F– and I– enrichment. This study demonstrates how transparent and reproducible AI tools can enhance groundwater-quality prediction and guide sustainable water management in large alluvial plains and other data-scarce, hydrogeochemically complex regions.

title: Sorption of metals and metalloids in hydraulic fracturing flowback water to surficial sediments
description: Publication date: Available online 2 September 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry Author(s): Sean P. Funk, Katherine N. Snihur, Konstantin von Gunten, Logan Swaren, Greg G. Goss, Daniel S. Alessi
abstract: The use of hydraulic fracturing techniques to liberate hydrocarbons from unconventional, tight formations, has increased in the past two decades. Of environmental concerns raised about the process, the potential impact of the wastewater recovered from these operations, called flowback water (FBW), is among the most discussed. FBW is a complex fluid, containing numerous inorganic and organic constituents, many of which may be highly mobile in the subsurface and can pose potential risks to near-surface ecosystems. Components of the fluid may interact with each other, either synergistically or antagonistically, resulting in varied sorption behavior, and furthermore, transient effects induced by groundwater flow may also impact these reactions. In this study, batch and column experiments were conducted using FBW (TDS 145,000 – 168,000 mg/L) and sediments collected from a region of hydraulic fracturing operations in west-central Alberta. In our batch experiments, we found that for many of the dissolved inorganic compounds (e.g. Sr, Cu, and Ni), sorption was depressed, likely a result of competition with other constituents within the fluid and the high ionic strength of the FBW. Column experiments were also conducted to address how groundwater flow may influence sorption, and it was found that some dissolved inorganic constituents (e.g. Sr, Li, and B) exhibited depressed sorption compared to the batch experiments. We argue that sorption is characterized by two stages: a fast adsorption phase onto external sorption sites, followed by a slow absorption phase into internal sorption sites, with the latter process negated by groundwater flow. However, metals exhibited enhanced retention in the presence of flow, possibly due to the anaerobic conditions in the column and precipitation of heavy metal-bearing solids sequestered these elements. Our results demonstrate the importance and need to consider both the full complexity found in real, field-collected FBW samples as well as groundwater flow, as co-contaminant interactions can have profound impact on the sorption behavior of individual solution components. Our results also suggest that many of the dissolved metals in FBW are likely highly mobile in the subsurface. This indicates that retention of these metals, even in high organic matter and high clay-content soils (which should act as a sink), is likely to be minimal, suggesting that if released into the environment, FBW may pose a risk to down-gradient ecosystems.

title: Mineralogy and Elemental Geochemistry of Coal Seams from underground fire-affected Jharia coal fields: Environmental Significance
description: Publication date: Available online 28 August 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry Author(s): Sukalyan Chakraborty, Wasim Akram Shaikh, Robert Barry Finkelman, Abhishek Kumar, Naomi Ty Asha Nichols
abstract: Uncontrolled coal fires in the Jharia coalfield, India, are examples of one of the worst forms of anthropogenic pollution, as they introduce a broad range of geotoxic compounds into the environment. This study examined the occurrence and distribution of fluoride and heavy metals in fire-affected villages of the Jharia region in various environmental media - coal, soil, plants, condensates/ sublimates, standing water, and foliar dust. The levels of fluoride were extraordinary, 411-622 mg kg-1 in coal, 166-147,333 mg kg-1 in condensates, 328-415mg kg-1 in soils, and 134-150 mg L-1 in water samples- way above the normal levels found in the environment. Fe (up to 37,070 mg kg-1), and Zn (268-449 mg kg-1) were highly enriched, and Mn, Mg, Cr, Cu, and Pb were moderately enriched. Geo-statistical indices showed that there is extreme Fe pollution (Igeo = 6.44-7.43) and moderate Zn contamination (Igeo = 1.09-1.30), PLI value (1.59-2.23). The highest bioaccumulation factor (BAF) for fluoride was observed in Ageratum conyzoides (9.34) and Croton bonplandianum (5.47), indicating that they are potential accumulator. The results indicate that during combustion of coal, volatilized minerals, such as fluorapatite, contribute to extensive contamination of the atmosphere and soil in the immediate vicinity, posing a high ecological and human health risk, particularly in areas with high concentrations in the condensates. Further, the hazard quotients and hazard indices (HI) were <1, indicating no significant non-carcinogenic health risk under the assessed exposure conditions. In addition, the elevated carcinogenic risk was observed in some selected condensate samples. There should be continuous monitoring and remediation measures that will reduce fluoride and heavy metal exposure in this susceptible coal-mining area.

title: “Geochemical processes at environmental interfaces”: A special issue in honor of Professor Guojiang Wan (1940-2016)

title: Geochemical distribution and mineralogical control of scandium in karst bauxite, NW Sardinia, Italy
description: Publication date: 5 November 2026 Source: Chemical Geology, Volume 723 Author(s): Alfredo Idini, Paola Mameli, Giovanni Mongelli, Emanuela Schingaro, Guido Cerri, Maria Lacalamita, Ernesto Mesto, Amid Ouladmansour, Matteo Luca Deidda, Stefano Naitza, Giacomo Oggiano
abstract: In the last years, karst bauxite have attracted considerable attention as secondary sources of critical metals, including scandium and, in this respect, we investigated the geochemical pathways of scandium in karst bauxites from the Nurra district, north-west Sardinia (Italy). The Nurra karst bauxite mainly consist of boehmite, goethite, hematite, kaolinite, and anatase. In the whole-rock the average Sc concentration is 51 mg/kg. Microanalysis show that Sc is, by far, hosted in Fe-rich domains where the average Sc content is 171 mg/kg. An unusual content of Zr is measured all along the micro analyses, dispersed ubiquitously in both Fe-rich domains and Al-rich domains. The distribution of Sc and Zr in neoformed structures, such as Fe–“agate” and Fe-veins, suggests that these elements were mobile during the formation of these textural components. The Nurra bauxite hosts three main zircon populations of different age that are disrupted, fractured and corroded. Only one zircon population has been identified as the main Sc host (from 1184 to 4164 Sc mg/kg). We suggest that the source of Sc in the Nurra bauxite comes from the partial dissolution of the Sc-rich zircon since: (i) no other Sc-bearing primary mineral has been detected; (ii) the UCC-like parent material and (iii) the Zr content dispersed in all the bauxite micro domains suggesting that Zr may experience a significant degree of mobility during bauxitization. On these basis, further studies are needed to investigate the pH oscillations during karst bauxite formation and their implications on the geochemical mobility of critical elements.

title: Experimental coefficients for the partitioning of Zn between dolomite and brine at 125 to 200° C
description: Publication date: 5 November 2026 Source: Chemical Geology, Volume 723 Author(s): Sarah E. Smith-Schmitz, Martin S. Appold, Hector M. Lamadrid
abstract: The concentration of Zn in aqueous fluids fundamentally affects the origin of sediment-hosted base metal ore deposits. Zinc concentration in ancient aqueous fluids can in principle be determined by direct measurement in fluid inclusions, from solubility theory, or by comparison to analogous modern fluids. However, attempts to employ these approaches are commonly hindered by uncertainties in how to interpret fluid inclusion analyses, uncertainties in the values of pH, redox potential, or sulfur concentration, or the compositional heterogeneity of modern crustal fluids. Partitioning theory provides a potential alternate way of determining Zn concentrations in aqueous fluids from measured Zn concentrations in a mineral that precipitated from that fluid, like dolomite, a common ore-stage mineral in sediment-hosted base metal deposits. The present study was undertaken to determine experimental partition coefficients (D) for the partitioning of Zn between water and dolomite under typical sediment-hosted base metal ore formation conditions. To this end, a series of dolomite precipitation experiments was performed at temperatures of 125, 150, 175, and 200 °C, pressures of 10 MPa and the saturation pressure of the aqueous solution, and Zn concentrations of 10, 100, and 1000 ppm for experimental durations of 10 to 80 days. Powder X-ray diffraction analysis of the resultant mineral precipitates indicates that they all consist predominantly of dolomite. Measured Zn/Mg ratios in the precipitates and the fluids were used to calculate D values of 42.1 ± 6.3, 30.5 ± 4.5, 20.7 ± 5.6, and 43.2 ± 9.2 at temperatures of 125, 150, 175, and 200 °C, respectively.

title: Variation of K-rich magma formation during early Aegean arc migration, NE Greece
description: Publication date: 5 November 2026 Source: Chemical Geology, Volume 723 Author(s): J.P.M. Wolf, K.M. Haase, M. Regelous, J. Falkenberg, E.M. Hars, P. Voudouris
abstract: Magmatic activity in the Aegean region has migrated southward by ∼400 km over the past ∼34 Ma due to rollback of the subducting African plate, producing age-progressive magmatic centres. In NE Greece, its earliest stage is recorded in the Maronia Magmatic Corridor, where magmatism between ∼34 and 29 Ma evolved from calc-alkaline in the northeast to shoshonitic compositions in the southwest. We present new major-element, trace-element (n = 67), and Sr-Nd-Pb-isotope (n = 36) data for volcanic and plutonic rocks to investigate magma generation and evolution during early Aegean arc migration. The magmatic rocks define geochemically distinct calc-alkaline and shoshonitic suites. The most mafic samples (4–10 wt.% MgO) show higher (Ce/Yb)N ratios in the shoshonite suite (10.8 ± 2.0) than the older calc-alkaline suite (5.5 ± 1.1), accompanied by distinct mean 206Pb/204Pbi ratios (18.68 ± 0.04 vs. 18.78 ± 0.03). Both suites evolved along coherent fractional-crystallisation ± assimilation trends, although the shoshonitic magmas show mantle-source heterogeneity. Lavas with transitional compositions (206Pb/204Pbi: 18.73 ± 0.01) bridge the two suites. Volcanic and plutonic rocks within individual centres display geochemical similarities, indicating common parental magmas and interconnected plumbing systems. Elevated P₂O₅ contents in transitional (0.4 ± 0.1 wt.%) and shoshonitic (0.6 ± 0.2 wt.%) magmas reflect increasing contribution from phosphorus-rich shallow-marine sediments, distinct from the pelagic sediments dominating the older calc-alkaline magmas. Our results show that changes in subducted pelagic-to-shallow-marine sediment input during slab rollback control K-enrichment in early Aegean arc magma generation, offering a geochemical framework for identifying discrete slab compositional inputs in migrating arc systems.

title: Variations of F-Cl-Br-I in the Pinghe alkaline complex (South China): Constraints on halogen budgets of the metasomatized lithospheric mantle
description: Publication date: 20 October 2026 Source: Chemical Geology, Volume 722 Author(s): Dan-Zhen Ma, Lian-Xun Wang, Sebastian Tappe, Yu-Xiang Zhu, Zhen-Bing She, Chao Zhang
abstract: The subcontinental lithospheric mantle (SCLM), modified by subducted oceanic components, acts as a major reservoir for deep-Earth halogens. This study investigates the halogen geochemistry (F, Cl, Br, I) of the alkaline rocks from Pinghe (South China) to constrain halogen behaviour during mantle metasomatism and subsequent magmatic-to-hydrothermal processes. Bulk-rock geochemical trends demonstrate that primitive lithologies (jacupirangite and ijolite) are characterized by high F (up to 2449 ppm) but relatively low Cl and Br contents. Conversely, more evolved lithologies (sodalite urtite and syenites) exhibit pronounced enrichment in Cl (up to 1253 ppm) and Br (up to 2.53 ppm). Mineral compositional analyses and element mapping reveal that fluorapatite is the primary F-host in jacupirangite and syenite, whereas biotite dominates the F-budget in ijolite and sodalite urtite. In contrast, Cl is partitioned into amphibole (jacupirangite and amphibole syenite), biotite (ijolite and nepheline syenite), and sodalite (urtite). Notably, the F contents of apatite decrease from jacupirangite to ijolite but increase in the most evolved suite, showing an antithetic relationship with Cl. This apparent decoupling is driven by extensive fractionation of fluorapatite, which sequesters F into cumulates and drives the residual melts toward progressive enrichment in Cl and Br, a signature recorded by the late-stage crystallization of Cl-rich amphibole and biotite. Despite the coupled behaviour of Cl and Br (mean Cl/Br of 540, excluding outliers), the F/Cl ratios vary by over three orders of magnitude due to the competing effects of early fluorapatite fractionation and late-stage sodalite crystallization. The combination of elevated halogen/Nb ratios (e.g., Cl/Nb up to 894), robust positive correlations between Ba/Nb and halogen/Nb, and distinctly low Br/Cl and I/Cl, indicates that the SCLM had been metasomatized by aqueous fluids derived from subducted altered oceanic crust and serpentinite. This study highlights that extreme halogen fractionation can occur during alkaline magma evolution, and our findings suggests that the least-evolved peralkaline melts carry a halogen signature inherited from a continental lithospheric mantle source pervasively metasomatized by slab-derived fluids.

title: Insights into the sulfur cycle in the Southern Tethys upwelling belt across the Cretaceous-Paleogene boundary
description: Publication date: 20 October 2026 Source: Chemical Geology, Volume 722 Author(s): Sutapa Patra, Yoav Oved Rosenberg, Alon Amrani
abstract: The Golan section of the southern Tethys upwelling belt is an organic and sulfur-rich section that records the K-Pg mass extinction interval. Geochemical and biomarker proxies indicate that the composition of the microbial and primary producer communities remained largely unchanged across the K-Pg boundary. This resilient behavior has been attributed to the long-term stratification and persistent euxinic conditions in the paleo-basin. Here, we investigate the impact of the K-Pg mass extinction event on sulfur cycling and organic matter (OM) preservation using the molecular and sulfur isotopic distribution of organic sulfur compounds (OSCs) and Fe speciation. Relationships among reactive Fe, S/Corg ratios, and sulfur isotopes of pyrite and organic sulfur indicate that excess sulfide preferentially reacted with OM, generating isotopically diverse OSCs. Redox proxies, combined with biomarkers for photic zone euxinia and hypersalinity, show that the basin remained strongly stratified and euxinic throughout the extinction interval. Most OSCs do not show significant variation in both concentration and δ34S values across the K-Pg boundary of the Golan section, consistent with the non‑sulfurized biomarkers, indicating a limited environmental perturbation. Nevertheless, OSCs show large isotopic variability (up to ∼12‰) reflecting differences in depositional conditions and preservation pathways. Benzo- and di-benzothiophenes preserve early diagenetic δ34S signatures despite being affected by early thermal maturation. Furthermore, n-alkylthiolanes are 5–9‰ 34S-enriched relative to bulk kerogen, indicating secondary and later sulfurization, whereas polycyclic terpenoid sulfides are comparatively 34S-depleted and interpreted as early diagenetic products. These compounds also exhibit concentration and isotopic shifts (∼6‰ 34S-depletion) in the post-extinction interval, highlighting their sensitivity to paleoenvironmental perturbations. In summary, this study shows a stable sulfur cycle and OM preservation across the K-Pg interval of the Golan Section. This, in turn, supports the resilience of biogeochemical cycles in the Southern Tethys upwelling belt despite the K-Pg crisis.

title: Compositional dependence of molar absorptivities for infrared absorption bands of H 2 O in rhyolitic to peridotitic glasses
description: Publication date: 20 October 2026 Source: Chemical Geology, Volume 722 Author(s): Dmitry Bondar, Anthony C. Withers, Danilo Di Genova, Alessio Zandonà, Hélène Bureau, Hicham Khodja, Alexander Kurnosov, Hongzhan Fei, Tomoo Katsura
abstract: Fourier transform infrared spectroscopy is widely used for H2O measurements in natural and synthetic silicate glasses. Previous calibrations focused on relatively polymerized compositions from rhyolitic to basanitic (non-bridging oxygen per tetrahedral cation ratios (NBO/T): 0–1.4), while we extend this range to highly depolymerized peridotitic glasses (NBO/T: 2.2–2.9). Bulk H2O contents of 0.3 to 4.7 wt% were determined by elastic recoil detection analysis, a reliable direct method for absolute hydrogen quantification; IR calibration used 10 samples with 1.8–4.7 wt%, excluding 0.3 wt%. We determined integrated molar absorption coefficients for the OH band at 4500 cm−1 ( ε ∗ O H = 124 ± 10 L mol−1 cm−2) and derived those for the H2O band at 5200 cm−1 assuming ε ∗ H 2 O / ε ∗ O H = 0.83 from the literature ( ε ∗ H 2 O = 103 ± 8 L mol−1 cm−2). Additionally, we determined linear and integrated molar absorption coefficients for the fundamental O–H stretching vibration band at 3530 cm−1, and its first overtone at 7030 cm−1. We compiled and critically assessed over 350 published molar absorption coefficients, creating the largest available database. This database includes glass compositions, water contents with analytical techniques, and baseline subtraction procedures, enabling identification of methodological biases and consistency across studies. Combined with our measurements, these data reveal that molar absorption coefficients for all four infrared bands correlate systematically with compositional parameters such as SiO2 mol% and decrease with increasing depolymerization. These trends, supported by theoretical considerations, enable prediction of molar absorption coefficients as a function of glass composition and accurate water quantification across a wide range of silicate glasses.

title: Response of mercury in sediments to environmental change in the Western Arctic Ocean since the late last deglaciation
description: Publication date: 20 October 2026 Source: Chemical Geology, Volume 722 Author(s): Song Zhao, Chao Cui, Weibin Zhang, Yanguang Liu
abstract: Since the last deglaciation, the western Arctic Ocean shelf has undergone a dramatic environmental transition from subaerial exposure to marine inundation. Permafrost, widely formed across the Arctic during the Last Glacial Maximum and acting as a vast reservoir of both organic carbon and mercury (Hg) during glacial periods, is highly sensitive to climate warming. The opening of the Bering Strait and the associated sea-level rise since the Late Pleistocene have fundamentally reshaped the sedimentary environment of the Chukchi Sea, which in turn influenced the burial and redistribution of Hg. However, how sedimentary Hg records have responded to this process remains unclear. This study analyzes a sediment core from the Chukchi Sea shelf in the western Arctic Ocean, spanning approximately the last 13 ka, to reconstruct the long-term evolutionary history of Hg burial fluxes. Our results reveal that, sedimentary Hg fluxes in the Chukchi Sea shelf increased by a factor of 4.4 from the last deglaciation to the late Holocene, primarily driven by the combined effects of remobilized Hg release, enhanced burial, and increased deposition. The region experienced two distinct peaks in Hg release during the early and late Holocene, driven by fundamentally different mechanisms. The early Holocene peak primarily resulted from the release and burial of Hg associated with permafrost organic carbon during transgression, coupled with extensive coastal erosion and thermokarst activity. The second, the Hg flux peak was closely linked to sea-ice retreat events driven by enhanced Pacific Water inflow during the late Holocene. Increased advection of warm Pacific waters extended the open-water season, enhancing the efficiency of the biological pump. This, in turn, facilitated the scavenging of water-column Hg by marine-derived organic carbon and likely enhanced the oceanic uptake of atmospheric Hg(0), thereby boosting the overall marine Hg sink. We note, however, that owing to the finite and trace nature of Hg in the environment, Hg burial might have been primarily supply-limited, potentially making the Hg flux less sensitive to environmental changes during periods of low atmospheric/oceanic Hg availability. The pre-anthropogenic natural background record revealed in this study elucidates the stepwise response of Hg burial on the Arctic shelf to climate forcing. It highlights the response of permafrost activation and ocean biogeochemical dynamics in governing the burial fate of this pollutant, providing a historical analog for assessing the evolution of the Arctic Hg.

title: Hydrothermal activity in the Eocene rift lake of the Beibuwan Basin, South China Sea: Mineralogical and geochemical constraints from lacustrine mudrocks
description: Publication date: 20 October 2026 Source: Chemical Geology, Volume 722 Author(s): Jiahao He, Qian Huang, Dujie Hou, Xinde Xu, Xiong Cheng, Gang Zhou, Weijun He
abstract: Hydrothermal fluids are important carriers of material and energy exchange among Earth spheres, yet well-documented records of their activity in ancient lacustrine basins remain limited. We conducted backscattered electron-energy dispersive X-ray spectroscopy imagery, elemental geochemical and strontium isotope analysis of Eocene lacustrine mudrocks from the Beibuwan Basin (BBWB). The results show that the shales contain abundant euhedral pyrite aggregates, chalcopyrite, native gold, siderite, and euhedral dolomite, indicating syngenetic hydrothermal activity. Coordinated positive excursions in Fe, Mn, P, Cu, Ba and Zn concentrations, paired with positive europium anomalies (δEu), record two short-lived diffuse flow events in the lower member of the Liushagang Formation (LS3) and a focused flow following deposition of the middle member of the Liushagang Formation (LS2). Tectonic analysis suggests that the remote effects of the India-Eurasia collision at ∼50 Ma potentially triggered basement fault activity, creating favorable pathways for hydrothermal fluid migration. Cross-plot of Fe/Ti versus Al/(Al + Fe + Mn) indicates that mudrocks near the basement faults received 20–50% hydrothermal contributions, whereas samples farther from the faults received less than 20%. Sr isotope compositions suggest that the hydrothermal fluids are of the crustal source, and identify two fluid endmembers. One is a high-temperature, reducing, sulfide-rich fluid associated with the syngenetic faults. The other is a carbonate-rich fluid formed in the depocenter via mixing with Upper Paleozoic limestone basement and lacustrine water. Tectonic activity and fault distribution are the main controlling factors for the source and migration of the two fluid types. This study fills the research gap of Eocene hydrothermal activity in the BBWB for the first time. It also provides an analog for hydrothermal sedimentation studies in the South China Sea and other rift lacustrine basins worldwide.

title: Redox and hydrodynamic controls on roll-front sandstone-type uranium mineralization: Insights from reactive transport modeling
description: Publication date: 20 October 2026 Source: Chemical Geology, Volume 722 Author(s): Yongqiang Zou, Zenghua Li, Teng Deng, Chiheng Liu, Yinhang Cheng, Deru Xu, Fei Xia, Lifei Yang
abstract: Roll-front sandstone-type uranium deposits are important uranium resources worldwide, but their orebodies vary significantly in location, geometry and grade despite broadly similar redox-controlled mineralization processes. This variability is attributed to differences in redox conditions, uranium source availability and groundwater flow, yet how these geological factors control orebody variability under hydrodynamic regimes remains poorly constrained. This study is the first to use reactive transport modeling to reproduce the dynamic process of roll-front uranium mineralization and to evaluate the effects of different geological factors on uranium orebody formation. The modeling results demonstrate that the dynamic balance between the reducing capacity of host sandstones and the oxidizing capacity of fluids exerts primary control on the localization, geometry and lateral extent of roll-front orebodies. Both strongly reducing host sandstones and weakly oxidizing fluids can limit interlayer oxidation, favoring narrow, relatively high-grade roll-front orebodies near the recharge area. In contrast, weakly reducing host sandstones and more oxidizing fluids allow significant interlayer oxidation, producing larger but relatively lower-grade mineralized zones farther from the recharge area. The uranium concentration in the fluids and the pre-enriched uranium content of the host sandstones are positively correlated with ore grade and together exert a primary control on the formation of high-grade roll-front uranium orebodies. Groundwater flow rate also exerts a non-linear influence on uranium mineralization, with moderate flow rates most favorable for uranium dissolving in the oxidization zone and reprecipitation at the redox front. Extremely low flow rates limit oxidation-front advance, whereas high flow rates promote extensive oxidation. These findings help explain the geological controls on orebody localization, geometry, and grade variability in roll-front uranium systems and provide a quantitative framework to guide future exploration.

title: Significant boron isotopic variations during crustal reworking recorded in multiple generations of tourmaline in S-type granites, South China
description: Publication date: 20 October 2026 Source: Chemical Geology, Volume 722 Author(s): Wei Li, Shuyun Cao, Eizo Nakamura, Zhong Liu, Tsutomu Ota, Yanlong Dong, Tak Kunihiro
abstract: Metamorphic dehydration and partial melting during crustal reworking play a critical role in the recycling of elements in collisional orogens. While boron (B) has great advantages in deciphering these fluid-related processes, its behavior during sequential evolution of multistage melts/fluids is not fully understood. Here, we investigate these processes through comprehensive analyses of major-trace elements and B isotopes of tourmaline in well-characterized S-type granites from the South China Block (SCB). Different occurrences of tourmaline have been identified, including (i) isolated tourmaline crystals and/or radiating tourmaline clusters with complex zoning pattern (Tur-Ia), (ii) isolated tourmaline crystals with patchy zoning pattern (Tur-Ib), (iii) loosely aggregated tourmaline crystals with complex zoning pattern in tourmaline aggregates (Tur-IIa), and (iv) densely tourmaline aggregated crystals with core-rim zoning pattern in tourmaline aggregates (Tur-IIb). Multiple generations of tourmalines with different origins display clear differences in texture, element, and B isotopic isotopes. Early-magmatic tourmaline is texturally and compositionally homogeneous with Mg/(Mg + Fe) = 0.21 to 0.53, while late-magmatic tourmaline has lower Mg/(Mg + Fe) = 0.03 to 0.44. Tourmaline of fluid origin, which is characterized by dissolution-reprecipitation texture and oscillatory zoning, has a large compositional range with Mg/(Mg + Fe) = 0.02 to 0.87. Chemical compositions of magmatic tourmaline were predominantly controlled by fractional crystallization, while chemical variations of tourmaline of fluid origin are mainly attributed to interaction of magma-derived hydrothermal fluids with metasedimentary rocks and/or addition of Mg-rich external fluids, in part because of the recharge of magma-derived Fe-rich hydrothermal fluids. The δ11B values are in the range of −11.8 ∼ −9.6‰ for early-magmatic tourmaline, in the range of −10.1 ∼ −6.7‰ for late-magmatic tourmaline and in the range of −14.5 ∼ −4.6‰ for tourmaline of fluid origin. We attribute the bimodal distribution of magmatic tourmaline δ11B to the occurrence of multistage tourmaline precipitation during magma differentiation to form an increase in the δ11B of tourmaline crystalized in later stages that assumes a Rayleigh fractionation. The varied B isotopes of tourmaline of fluid origin are controlled by the increase in δ11B formed by boron-isotope fractionation and the decrease in δ11B formed by addition of low δ11B external dehydration fluids, as evidenced by the elemental characteristics of tourmaline of fluid origin with low δ11B and model calculation of B behavior. On this basis, we propose a model where post-collision extension led to metamorphic dehydration of metasedimentary rocks, with the resultant metamorphic fluids not only migrating upward and interacting with overlying metasedimentary rocks to generate a metasomatic source that subsequently underwent dehydration melting to produce granitic melts, but also participating in fluid activity in later stages. A spatiotemporally coupled metamorphic dehydration-partial melting mechanism may result in locally variable B isotope values in syn- and post-collisional magmas through melt-fluid-rock interaction and fluid mixing.

title: Zn isotopic evidence for the role of recycled sedimentary carbonate in generating carbonatites and alkaline rocks associated with rare-metal mineralization
description: Publication date: 20 October 2026 Source: Chemical Geology, Volume 722 Author(s): Juan Wang, Ling Han, Peilong Cui, Yu Kang, Shuaijun Wang, Ganglan Zhang, Xiangfa Wang
abstract: Carbon is crucial to the genesis of carbonatites and alkaline rocks associated with rare metal deposits, yet its origin remains poorly constrained. Here we present an integrated study of petrography, titanite U-Pb geochronology, and whole-rock geochemistry (major and trace elements, Sr-Nd-Zn isotopes) to evaluate the role of recycled sedimentary carbonate in the generation of carbonatite-syenite complex from the Miaoya Nb-REE deposit and the alkaline volcanic rocks from the Yehuzhai Nb deposit, which are spatially related in the South Qinling (SQ) region. The combined titanite U-Pb ages, major and trace elements, and Sr-Nd isotopes indicate that these carbonatites and alkaline rocks were derived from a mantle metasomatized by oceanic crust-derived melts/fluids and formed in an early Paleozoic extensional tectonic setting linked to the opening of the Mianlue Ocean. The Miaoya complex exhibits a wide range of δ66Zn values from 0.29‰ to 0.44‰, with some values higher than those of MORB. A two-end-member mixing model suggests that up to 25% of recycled sedimentary carbonate was incorporated into the mantle source. In contrast, the Yehuzhai alkaline rocks yield MORB-like δ66Zn values (0.29–0.36‰), which can be explained by partial melting of peridotitic mantle with negligible contribution from sedimentary carbonate. The contrasting Zn isotopic signatures reflect the varying degree of recycled carbonate contribution to the mantle heterogeneity beneath the SQ region. Collectively, these findings highlight a genetic relationship among deep carbon cycle, tectonic activity, carbonatite-alkaline rocks generation, and rare metal mineralization.

title: Time-dependent intensity corrections for accurate quantitative point or X-ray mapping analysis by electron microprobe
description: Publication date: 20 October 2026 Source: Chemical Geology, Volume 722 Author(s): Julien M. Allaz, Anette von der Handt, John J. Donovan
abstract: Many materials undergo modifications to both structure and chemistry during electron bombardment in an electron probe microanalyzer (EPMA). This results in changes to the emitted X-ray intensities by various physical processes including heating, breaking of molecular bonds, ionization, volatilization and sputtering, subsurface static charging and subsequent mobility of the measured elements. Most of these processes are proportional to the degree and duration of electron beam exposure (analytical time, acceleration voltage, beam current, and beam focus) and to the thermal and electrical conductivity of the analyzed material. Therefore, quantitative accuracy is dependent upon correction schemes that monitor changes in X-ray emission over time, a process called Time-Dependent Intensity (TDI) corrections. This paper investigates various applications of TDI corrections and demonstrates that accurate point analyses can be obtained with such corrections. Moreover, the combination of replicate X-ray mapping with a TDI correction can produce precise and accurate quantitative element maps for beam-sensitive materials, expanding the range of materials and analytical conditions suitable for EPMA applications.

title: The selenium cycling variation corresponding to the evolution of early animals in the Weng'an biota
description: Publication date: 20 October 2026 Source: Chemical Geology, Volume 722 Author(s): Zhiyuan Ren, Jie Long, Shixi Zhang, Yajun Du, Tengwen Long, Yung-Tsang Chen, Kunli Luo
abstract: The Weng'an biota witnessed the critical expansion and differentiation of early animals in the Ediacaran Period. It shows an enrichment of bioessential elements such as Se and Mo accompanying the expansion of Megasphaera fossils. However, whether the expansion of early animals affected the Se source and its preservation remains unclear. This research focuses on studying the Se speciation and preservation variations in the Weng'an biota along with the occurrence, expansion, and disappearance of Megasphaera fossils and the covariation of redox conditions. Before the Megasphaera occurrence, it shows 14.5% of bioavailable Se(VI) and Se(IV) (29 ppb), 2% (up to 13 ppb) of Se(0), 57% (56 ppb) of Se(II) and 26.5% (40 ppb) of organic Se (Org-Se). The bioavailable Se(VI) and Se(IV) increased to 35% (160–8000 ppb) in the first occurrence datum of Megasphaera while the Se(0), Se(-II), and Org-Se decreased to 1% (155 ppb), 54% (7800 ppb), and 10% (1500 ppb) respectively. The Se(VI) + Se(IV) and Se(-II) changed to 46% (10,000 ppb) and 40% (9200 ppb) respectively within the acme interval of Megasphaera while the proportions of Se(0) and Org-Se remained similar to the occurrence layer. In the decline interval, the Se(VI) + Se(IV), Se(-II) and Org-Se varied to 9% (8 ppb), 76% (56 ppb), and 15% (40 ppb) respectively while the Se(0) became undetectable. After excluding the effects of terrestrial input and hydrothermal activities, we proposed that the Se cycling variation in the Weng'an biota was highly probably related to the evolution of Megasphaera.

title: Competing effects of mantle melting, magma crystallization and degassing on sulfur, chalcophile, and siderophile elements in volcanic glasses from Shatsky Rise and Ojin Rise seamounts
description: Publication date: 20 October 2026 Source: Chemical Geology, Volume 722 Author(s): Maxim Portnyagin, Renat Almeev, Jörg Geldmacher, Roman Botcharnikov, Dieter Garbe-Schönberg
abstract: Oceanic large igneous provinces (LIPs), such as Shatsky Rise in the western Pacific, commonly exhibit variable and locally elevated abundances of chalcophile and siderophile elements (CSEs), reflecting the conditions of mantle melting and subsequent magma differentiation. However, the processes and conditions controlling these enrichments remain poorly understood. To unravel these processes, we analyzed major, volatile, and trace elements, including the strongly chalcophile and siderophile trace and ultra-trace elements Cu, Ag, Se, Re, Pt, Au, and Bi, in 48 glass samples from Shatsky Rise and the adjacent Ojin Rise seamounts. We also determined Fe3+/ΣFe ratios in 19 glasses and measured major element and sulfur contents in plagioclase-hosted melt inclusions from the Tamu Massif, the oldest in the Shatsky Rise. Parental Shatsky Rise magmas are strongly enriched in CSEs relative to MORB. They are inferred to have formed at logfO2 of FMQ to FMQ − 1 and to have evolved by fractional crystallization, resulting in auto-oxidation to as high as FMQ + 1 in the most evolved melts. The CSE patterns of the normal-type Shatsky Rise magmas are consistent with extensive (22–25%) mantle plume melting that exhausted sulfide from the mantle residue. In contrast, parental Ojin magmas resemble MORB and became sulfide-saturated during the early stages of fractional crystallization. They were likely generated by more moderate degrees of mantle melting, leaving a sulfide-bearing residue at logfO2 below FMQ. All Shatsky Rise melts remained sulfide-undersaturated during fractional crystallization down to ∼7 wt% MgO. At lower MgO, the glasses define two contrasting evolutionary trends: sulfur-rich, CSE-depleted, sulfide-saturated compositions from the Ori Massif and Ojin Rise seamounts, and sulfur-poor, CSE-enriched, slightly more oxidized, sulfide-undersaturated compositions from the Tamu Massif. Ori Massif magmas record little or no sulfur degassing during crystallization and eruption and remain to be sulfide-saturated. In contrast, Tamu magmas experienced substantial pre-eruptive sulfur loss within an open-vent magmatic system, where prolonged recycling and mixing of degassed and undegassed magmas progressively depleted the magma in sulfur. These results highlight the fundamental role of shallow magmatic processes in controlling CSEs behavior in oceanic plateau magmas and determine their potential for the formation of magmatic sulfide deposits. Sulfide undersaturation during shallow evolution diminishes the ore-forming potential of LIP magmas, whereas late-stage sulfide saturation favors formation of Au–Cu–PGE-rich but relatively Ni-poor magmatic sulfides.

title: Temporal variations in the Fe isotope composition of Arctic Ocean Fe-Mn crusts reflect iron sources and environmental conditions
description: Publication date: 20 October 2026 Source: Chemical Geology, Volume 722 Author(s): Natalia Konstantinova, Minako Kurisu, James R. Hein, Sergei Skolotnev, Georgy Cherkashov, Katsuhiko Suzuki
abstract: Layered ferromanganese crusts from Mendeleev Ridge and Northwind Ridge in the Arctic Ocean Amerasia Basin, and Vøring Spur and Knipovich Ridge in the North Atlantic Ocean constitute valuable archives of paleoenvironmental changes for the Arctic region. Temporal variation in δ56Fe isotope values of hydrogenetic Fe-Mn crusts from the deep Arctic Ocean vary from 0.00‰ to −0.44‰. Both Amerasia Basin Fe-Mn crusts show relatively heavy late Miocene δ56Fe values (0.00‰ to −0.12‰) followed by a decrease during the Pliocene–Pleistocene, likely reflecting increasing Fe contributions from redox reactions in continental-shelf sediments. The δ56Fe signatures in the uppermost layers of Fe-Mn crusts from the Mendeleev, Northwind and Knipovich Ridges are consistent and their reconstructed seawater compositions agree well with modern dissolved Fe isotope values from comparable depths in Canada Basin and Mendeleev Ridge. The Fe-Mn crust from Vøring Spur indicates a relatively constant Fe source from deep North Atlantic waters since the late Miocene.

title: Copper isotope evidence for Cu transfer during oceanic crust subduction: insights from the (ultra)high-pressure metamorphic belt of Southwestern Tianshan, China
description: Publication date: 20 October 2026 Source: Chemical Geology, Volume 722 Author(s): Yu Chen, Yuanyuan Xiao, Yongxiang Yao, Baptiste Debret, Ziwei Sun, Hongmei Gong, Yao Liu, Kaiyun Chen
abstract: Constraining the behavior of Cu during subduction is the key to decipher processes leading to the porphyry Cu deposit formation at convergent margins, while also shedding light on S cycling owing to the chalcophile affinity of Cu. This study reported δ65Cu values for bulk-rock and chalcopyrite from a metamafic rock from the (ultra-)high pressure metamorphic belt of Southwestern Tianshan, China. The rock consists of abundant glaucophane-dominated breccias (part A) crosscut by a large-scale omphacite-rich vein system (part B) with sharp boundaries. The glaucophane-dominated breccias are interpreted as partially dehydrated metabasalts, while the omphacite-rich vein system reflects the main fluid pathways in the subduction channel. Part A exhibits elevated δ65Cu values (0.07‰ to 0.36‰) and low Cu contents (52 ppm on average) compared to MORB (δ65Cu = 0.04‰ to 0.14‰; Cu = 90 ppm). Together with heavier δ65Cu values of chalcopyrite (−0.17‰ to 0.23‰) in part A compared to magmatic sulfide, these suggest that dehydration preferentially releases isotopically light Cu and leaves residues with heavier Cu isotope compositions. Part B shows complementary light δ65Cu values both in bulk rock and chalcopyrite. The negative correlation between S and δ65Cu indicates that precipitated sulfides complexed with light Cu isotopes may result in lowered δ65Cu values in the rock during fluid-rock interactions. Overall, the data point to the mobilization of isotopically light Cu-bearing fluids during the dehydration of mafic crust in subduction environments. However, the absence of commonly high Cu contents in arc magmas suggests that the released copper may be buffered by sulfides in the sub-arc mantle, resulting in Cu-rich sulfide accumulations.

title: Sulfide inclusions in phenocrysts from basanite lithic clasts and mafic phonolite lapilli from the Upper Laacher See Tephra (Germany): Evolution of an immiscible sulfide liquid
description: Publication date: 20 October 2026 Source: Chemical Geology, Volume 722 Author(s): Alexandre V. Andronikov, Irina E. Andronikova, Ondrej Pour, Gerhard Wörner
abstract: Sulfide inclusions in phenocrysts from phonolite lapilli from the Upper Laacher See Tephra (ca. 13 ka) along with basanite lithic clasts were analyzed in situ for major- and trace-element compositions using SEM and LA-ICP-MS techniques. For the first time, we trace the compositional evolution of trace elements in the Laacher See immiscible sulfide liquids that exsolved from the basanite and mafic phonolite melts at various stages of differentiation. Sulfide inclusions represent former immiscible sulfide liquids that exsolved from both basanite parent magma and evolved daughter phonolite melts. After their incorporation into host minerals, the inclusions in basanitic mafic phenocrysts evolved during ascent and cooling in dikes and/or lava flows. The resultant sulfide inclusions are always polymineralic and composed of Fe-, Cu-, and Ni-rich phases (mainly pyrrhotite, chalcopyrite, pentlandite). In contrast, sulfide inclusions in mafic and felsic phenocrysts in phonolite lapilli are almost pure, homogeneous pyrrhotite (Cu-Ni-poor phase) and have low content of Ni, Co, and Cu, but elevated concentrations of Cd, Pb, Te and Zn. Our data thus document a sequence of sulfide liquid exsolution that occurred along the differentiation path from basanite to phonolite magma.

title: Geochemical indicators of deep fluid dynamics in the Gulf of Patience (Sakhalin Island): new data on submarine mud volcanism and its connection with the region's tectonics
description: Publication date: 20 October 2026 Source: Chemical Geology, Volume 722 Author(s): Varvara Ivanova, Petr Semenov, Anna Kil, Vladimir Slinchenkov, Alexander Kartashev, Vyacheslav Sevastyanov, Boris Vanshtein
abstract: The article presents the results of a comprehensive geochemical monitoring of the underwater gas seep Vostochnoe (the Gulf of Patience, Sea of Okhotsk) in 2022–2025. Based on the analysis of the molecular and isotopic composition (δ13C) of hydrocarbon gases, the distribution of inorganic gases (He, CO₂) and trace elements (Zn, Hg, Cu, Co, Ni, etc.) in bottom sediments, the nature of the fluid system of this feature is characterized for the first time. The composition of gases and sediments of the site is consistent with potential genetic links to the processes feeding the Pugachevsky mud volcano on land, suggesting that the Vostochnoe site may represent its submarine continuation. However, key geochemical indicators (gas dryness coefficient K1, paraversity index K4, helium and mercury contents) suggest possible differences in the discharge mechanism: Vostochnoe is characterized by high thermodynamic maturity of gases, the absence of a typical hydrothermal trace element load, and episodic pulses of deep fluid enriched in helium. Particularly noteworthy is the 2024 anomaly, when a sharp increase in He concentrations (up to 184 ppm) and the appearance of thermogenic methane with δ13С up to −35.6‰ were recorded at several stations, suggesting possible short-term activation of a deep fault. However, these interpretations remain provisional; alternative explanations involving different reservoirs, regional source rocks, or mixing-fractionation effects cannot be excluded without further isotopic and structural studies.

title: Re -Os dating of paleozoic organic-rich black shales by LA-ICP-MS/MS
description: Publication date: 20 October 2026 Source: Chemical Geology, Volume 722 Author(s): Jay M. Thompson, Stijn Glorie, A. Kate Souders, Sarah E. Gilbert, Timothy Paton, Poul Emsbo
abstract: We present a new in-situ method for Re Os geochronology of black shales using LA-ICP-MS/MS that is rapid, cost-effective, and sufficiently accurate and precise to address many geological questions. The method is tested on Paleozoic organic-rich black shales with independently constrained stratigraphic or radiometric ages. Results demonstrate that LA-ICP-MS/MS analysis yields Re Os dates and initial Os isotopic compositions generally within uncertainty of published values using a laser spot size of 100 to 120 μm in diameter. Despite low Os abundances in many samples, high-density microscale sampling compensates through large numbers of analyses, enabling robust inverse isochron regressions. The approach also allows contemporaneous acquisition of trace-element data (V, Ni, Mo and Re), providing insight into metal distribution in a sample, degree of metal enrichments, and serve as a proxy for open-system behavior for Re Os. As a result, LA-ICP-MS/MS ReOs analysis can serve both as a stand-alone geochronological tool and as an efficient screening method prior to conventional ID-N-TIMS, helping to identify optimal intervals and exclude isotopically disturbed material. Together, our study demonstrates that in-situ Re Os geochronology of organic-rich shales is technically viable, geologically informative, and broadly applicable, opening new opportunities to investigate basin evolution, metallogenesis, hydrocarbon systems, and Earth-system processes across deep time.

title: Abundant and diverse Pb nanospheres in polyphase Eoarchean zircon from the Odesa Quarry, Ukrainian Shield
description: Publication date: 20 October 2026 Source: Chemical Geology, Volume 722 Author(s): Monika A. Kusiak, Simon A. Wilde, Richard Wirth, Leonid Shumlyanskyy, Bożena Gołębiowska, Martin J. Whitehouse
abstract: Nanoclusters and nanospheres of radiogenic lead (Pb*) have been recognized in zircon from several locations around the world, but their formation remains enigmatic. Here, we describe examples from the Odesa Quarry in Ukraine that reveal several unique features not previously identified, providing new insights into their origin. Here, randomly distributed Pb nanospheres (cubic crystals of metallic Pb) of various shapes and sizes are present in the cores and rims of zircon, both concordant and discordant, in an Eoarchean quartzitic rock. New features identified include metallic Ti6Pb4.8 (documented earlier only as an experimental product) and composite bodies consisting of Pb nanospheres together with either Ti clusters (in the zircon cores) or with Al (in the zircon rims). These bodies are up to 80 nm in size. In some rim domains, larger Pb nanospheres co-exist with an amorphous silica-rich phase (ASP), either enclosed in a silica globule or margined by silica. This association of Pb nanospheres with either Ti or Al is controlled by the different conditions of zircon growth experienced by the cores and recrystallization of the rims. Such a complexity of Pb mobilization, together with other elements, significantly advances our knowledge about zircon micro- and nanostructures.

title: Resolving two different mantle plume components in the Central Indian Ridge using olivine-hosted melt inclusions from a low-magma supply region
description: Publication date: 20 October 2026 Source: Chemical Geology, Volume 722 Author(s): Sunghwan Im, Jung-Woo Park, Sarang Choi, Jonguk Kim, Andrey A. Gurenko, Seongjun Choi
abstract: Two deep-mantle reservoirs branching from African LLSVP, the Réunion plume and Mascarene Basin Asthenospheric Reservoir (MBAR), have been proposed to influence magmatism along the Central Indian Ridge (CIR), yet distinct geochemical expression, spatial extents and relative contributions remain poorly constrained. In this study, we present major and trace element, volatile and in-situ Pb isotope data for olivine-hosted melt inclusions from a ridge-transform intersection at the CIR 16.5°S where low magma supply preserves primary mantle heterogeneity. The melt inclusions exhibit a broad range of trace element enrichment, collectively encompassing nearly the full compositional variability of the CIR MORB over a distance of ∼1000 km. The melt inclusions are categorized into three types: E-MORB, N-MORB and anomalous melt inclusions. Although some anomalous inclusions show geochemical evidence of interaction with the lower crust and upper mantle, most preserve their primary mantle source signatures. E-MORB melt inclusions exhibit Pb isotopic, halogen, major and trace element compositions suggesting mantle source metasomatized by low-degree melts derived from the Réunion plume. In contrast, N-MORB melt inclusions show restricted La/Sm but wide variability in Pb isotope ratios defining FOZO-DMM array, independent of the Réunion plume signatures. These geochemical characteristics suggests MBAR contribution extends southward to ∼16.5°S as previously inferred from geophysical data. The coexistence of the Réunion plume and MBAR signatures within individual melt inclusions suggests that melt inclusions provide critical role in resolving deep-mantle heterogeneity beneath the Indian Ocean while otherwise remaining cryptic in MORB whole-rocks or glasses, even in low-magma supply regions.

title: In situ iron isotopic analysis of mantle silicate minerals by fs-LA–MC–ICP–MS
description: Publication date: 20 October 2026 Source: Chemical Geology, Volume 722 Author(s): Xinting Lü, Detao He, Yongsheng Liu, Huajiang Liang, Chunfei Chen, Kexin Deng, Xi Zhu, Ming Li, Yansheng Lai, Ao Yang, Jie Lin, Zhaochu Hu
abstract: In situ iron isotope analysis of mantle silicate minerals (e.g., clinopyroxene, orthopyroxene, garnet) is essential for understanding mantle processes. However, existing mineral-scale Fe isotopic data for these phases are predominantly derived from bulk analysis of mineral separates, as in situ measurements are constrained by low iron contents, matrix effects and the lack of suitable reference materials for microbeam analysis. In this study, we present a high-precision method for in situ Fe isotope analysis of silicate minerals using a high-energy femtosecond laser ablation system (GenesisGEO) coupled with MC-ICP-MS. The improved sensitivity enables robust analysis of samples with FeO as low as ∼2.7 wt%. The isobaric interference from 54Cr is accurately corrected using pure Cr metal. Under optimized wet-plasma conditions, a suite of laboratory-synthesized clinopyroxene (CPXA01, CPXB01), orthopyroxene (OPX-GL3), and garnet (GRT-GL3) glasses, along with natural mantle minerals (ML OPX, CUG-OL-Ar, SC Ol), were accurately measured. All materials exhibit homogeneous Fe isotope compositions, making them suitable as in-house quality-control materials. The δ56Fe values obtained by fs-LA-MC-ICP-MS agree with solution data within uncertainty. External reproducibility (2SD) is better than 0.13‰ even at FeO contents below 3 wt%, demonstrating the robustness of the method for analyzing typical mantle silicate minerals. Applying this method to clinopyroxene and garnet from eclogite xenoliths reveals pronounced Fe isotope variability at the micrometer scale, demonstrating its capability to resolve microscale isotopic heterogeneity preserved in mantle minerals. This work extends high-precision in situ Fe isotope analysis from iron-rich sulfides and oxides to major silicate phases of the mantle, thereby enabling micron-scale studies of Fe isotope fractionation during mantle processes.

title: Deciphering the origin of ultrapotassic magmas in the North China Craton: Mg isotopic constraints on the roles of carbonates vs. pelagic clays
description: Publication date: 20 October 2026 Source: Chemical Geology, Volume 722 Author(s): Xiaolu Niu, Yildirim Dilek, Bin Chen, Fei Liu, Shan Ke, Guangying Feng, Jingsui Yang
abstract: The formation of ultrapotassic rocks in subduction zones is a direct consequence of mantle metasomatism by recycled sediments. However, the first-order control exerted by specific sedimentary components (e.g., carbonates vs. pelagic clays) on the compositional diversity of these magmas remains poorly constrained. To address this, we integrate Mg–O–Sr isotopes with elemental geochemistry on a suite of silica-saturated and silica-undersaturated ultrapotassic rocks from the northern North China Craton. These rocks form a coherent geochemical array, characterized by low Hf/Sm (mostly <1) and unradiogenic 87Sr/86Sr (0.705–0.708), alongside high Sr (1000–6000 ppm), Ba (up to 10,000 ppm), and CaO/Al2O3 ratios. This signature precludes a significant contribution from terrigenous sediments but is consistent with a mantle source containing both pelagic clays and carbonates. Critically, Mg isotopes systematically discriminate these sedimentary components. The silica-undersaturated Late Triassic rocks possess light δ26Mg values (−0.42‰ to −0.23‰), requiring modification of their mantle source by carbonatitic melts. In contrast, the silica-saturated Early Devonian rocks exhibit heavier δ26Mg values (−0.27‰ to −0.12‰), implicating pelagic clay as the dominant metasomatic agent. We thus establish a genetic linkage: ultrapotassic magmas from clay-modified sources are silica-saturated and have heavier δ26Mg, while those from carbonate-modified sources are silica-undersaturated and have lighter δ26Mg. This Mg-isotope dichotomy offers a powerful and novel means to trace sediment recycling and unravel the nature of mantle metasomatism in subduction zones.

title: Tracking of the origin and history of fluids in the Hellisheiði and Nesjavellir geothermal fields, Iceland
description: Publication date: 20 October 2026 Source: Chemical Geology, Volume 722 Author(s): Biying Chen, Finlay M. Stuart, Chris M. Holdsworth, Stuart M.V. Gilfillan
abstract: The geochemistry of geothermal fluids provides critical insights into their provenance and subsurface transport mechanisms, which are essential for exploration and sustainable exploitation of geothermal resources. Prolonged production and reinjection of wastewater might overprint original fluid chemistry, complicating reservoir characterisation. This study uses stable isotopes of water (δD, δ18O) and the noble gas composition of production fluids collected during multiple sampling campaigns at the Hellisheiði and Nesjavellir fields, Iceland, to evaluate fluid evolution during continuous production and reinjection. Comparison with pre-commissioning data indicates that water isotopic composition has remained stable, suggesting that production and reinjection have not significantly altered the primary fluid composition over 18 years at Hellisheiði and 34 years at Nesjavellir. The noble gas composition of most samples is consistent with phase separation. The temperature of phase separation constrained by noble gas compositions exceeds surface separator temperatures, suggesting that subsurface boiling has likely occurred. However, the estimated boiling temperatures are 29–145 °C lower than reservoir temperatures, implying that boiling occurs in the shallow subsurface or within the wellbores. This study also provides an evaluation of a Kr tracer test at Nesjavellir that was initiated in 2019, prior to CO2 injection.
